memory_leads.lead: A vessel or owner's local ship/port agent commonly acts as a coordination layer between master/operator, terminal, port authority and marine-service providers, translating ETA/readiness changes into local arrangements without itself being the authority for every service.

A berth window or berth-planning slot is a distinct readiness state from physical berth existence: late arrival, prolonged prior calls or priority changes can cause a vessel to miss an expected window and re-enter a queue.
Anchorage or roadstead waiting is a separate pre-berth operating state with queue, weather and service-access implications; port congestion can therefore accumulate outside the terminal footprint.

Harbor-master/VTS or analogous traffic-control functions coordinate vessel movements through channels, anchorages and port basins, so nautical traffic permission/sequencing is an operational constraint distinct from cargo-terminal readiness.

Pilot boarding and disembarkation create a physical transfer/readiness point before and after confined-water navigation; pilot availability, boarding location and weather/sea conditions can delay an otherwise ready vessel.

Pilotage capacity is itself a service pool with qualification and scheduling constraints. The structural memory is that local navigational expertise must be available at the needed time, while compulsory/exemption rules are port-specific and deferred.

Tug assistance forms another readiness pool: vessel size, maneuvering characteristics, berth geometry, weather and local practice can change the number/type of tugs needed, so tug availability can constrain arrival or departure independently of berth capacity.

Mooring and line-handling teams, boats or shore systems create a final interface between maneuvering vessel and berth; a ship can reach the berth area yet remain unable to complete all-fast/unmooring states on the desired schedule.

Tide, draft, under-keel-clearance and channel-depth constraints can create time windows for transit or sailing. Available berth depth and approach-channel eligibility must therefore be replayed as time-dependent readiness rather than one static vessel/port compatibility flag.

Narrow or traffic-constrained channels may require one-way sequencing, meeting restrictions or managed movement order, turning marine access into a shared schedule resource even when there is no cargo-handling bottleneck.

Weather and visibility can interrupt pilot transfers, tug/maneuvering operations or safe channel movement differently from terminal crane weather limits; port-call weather exposure is therefore multi-stage.

Shifting between berths, anchorages or terminals is a separate intra-port movement with pilot/tug/mooring and timing requirements; multi-terminal calls can accumulate marine-service delays between cargo operations.
Departure readiness is its own chain: cargo/terminal completion does not equal sailing because unmooring, tug/pilot readiness, traffic clearance and tide/channel eligibility may still have to align.

Port-stay time should be decomposed into pre-berth waiting, nautical/marine-service movement, berth occupation/cargo work and post-completion departure delay; one aggregate dwell number hides which capacity pool caused the delay.

P019 schedule reliability is refined by berth-window feedback: late arrival can miss a planned berth/pilot/tug sequence, producing additional waiting that makes the next call later still even without a new external disruption.

Vessel upsizing can raise marine-service and nautical-access requirements even when terminal cranes can physically reach the ship, so mega-ship scale can shift bottlenecks from cargo equipment toward channels, turning basins, tugs and time windows.

Anchorage waiting, maneuvering and schedule-recovery steaming connect port-call coordination to fuel/emissions economics; environmental cost can rise because of timing mismatch even when voyage distance is unchanged.
Channels, dredging, turning basins and berth-water-depth infrastructure were already captured in P021; P022 retains only their immediate time-dependent operational-readiness consequences.
Crane/gang/cargo-handling productivity at berth was already captured by P014; P022 stops at marine arrival/departure coordination rather than reopening the cargo-execution layer.

reviewed_no_specific_memory.reason: Local requirements and pricing vary by port, vessel class and period and require Evidence.
Blind memory supports berth/traffic sequencing as a category but not exact priority algorithms, notice periods or local harbor rules.
No reliable basis exists for exhaustive provider histories or rankings across ports and geographies.
Event-level attribution and timing require dated claim-scoped Evidence and are outside this blind structural pass.

stop_reason: The immediate port-call readiness chain is populated from agent/berth planning through anchorage, harbor/VTS sequencing, pilot/tug/mooring and tide/channel constraints to departure. Further recall becomes port-, provider-, tariff-, rule- or incident-specific.
truth_boundary: Memory-only orientation; no local pilotage/towage/mooring rule or tariff, berth priority, provider identity, channel restriction, port-call delay or historical incident is verified.
